payload.rationale: No forecast or observational data was supplied, so this estimate rests on climatology for Austin (Camp Mabry, the CLIAUS station) around September 19. The normal daily high in mid-to-late September is roughly 90-92°F, with a day-to-day standard deviation of about 5°F. A high of 98-99°F is roughly 1.5 standard deviations above normal; such readings occur in mid/late September during persistent ridging or late-season heat, but on a given day the climatological chance of landing exactly in the two-degree 98-99 bin is only about 7-10%. Rounding conventions (Weather Company reports whole degrees, so 97.5-99.4 effectively captures the bin) are already reflected in this band width. Reasons the estimate could be too high: late September often brings the first fronts or moisture that cap highs in the low 90s, and the bin is narrow, so even a warm regime could yield 96-97 or 100+. Reasons it could be too low: if 2026 features a hot, dry September pattern (as in several recent years such as 2023), highs near 98-100 become common, and the existence of this bracket suggests forecasts may be in the upper 90s, which could push the true probability to 25-40%. Without any current forecast, I weight climatology with a modest upward tilt for the possibility that the bracket is near the forecast center.
limitations: No forecast, observation, or model data supplied; estimate is climatological with a modest adjustment.
Unknown 2026 synoptic pattern, drought status, or heat regime for central Texas.
Two-degree bin makes the outcome sensitive to one-degree forecast errors and Weather Company rounding/revision practices.
Station-specific (CLIAUS/Camp Mabry) versus airport differences are not assessed.
